item.title: [Marketing 101 #11] Why the Same Pill Costs Twice as Much With a Name on It
item.body:
> A brand is a promise stored in someone's head — and brand management is the work of building that promise, keeping it consistent, and knowing how far you can stretch it before it snaps.

## Today's Concept

Walk into any store and you'll find two products that are physically close to identical, sitting side by side, with very different price tags. Nothing about the atoms explains the gap. Something about the *name* does.

That gap has a name in marketing: **brand equity** — the extra value a brand name adds beyond what the product itself delivers. One rough way to picture it:

```
Brand equity ≈ what people will pay for the branded version
             − what they'd pay for an identical unbranded version
```

That's a simplification (equity also shows up as loyalty, bargaining power with retailers, and cheaper customer acquisition), but it makes the idea concrete: equity is measurable, and it lives in the customer's mind, not on the factory floor.

Marketing academics usually break brand equity into four building blocks, following David Aaker's well-known model:

- **Awareness** — do people know you exist, and do you come to mind first?
- **Perceived quality** — do they believe you're good, whether or not lab tests agree?
- **Associations** — what images, feelings, and situations attach to the name?
- **Loyalty** — will they buy you again when a cheaper option is right there?

Now, the second concept. **Brand identity** is what the company *intends* the brand to stand for — the positioning, the personality, the visual system, the tone. **Brand image** is what customers *actually* believe. Those two are rarely the same thing, and closing the gap is most of a brand manager's job. You control the identity. You only influence the image.

Third: **brand extension**. Once a brand has equity, it's tempting to spend it — to launch a product in a new category under the same name and borrow the trust you've already earned. Extensions are cheap compared to building a brand from zero, and that's exactly why they're overused.

The variable that predicts success is **perceived fit**: does the new product feel like something this brand would plausibly make? Nike moving from shoes into athletic apparel fits. Apple moving from computers into phones fits. Harley-Davidson launching a perfume in the 1990s did not fit, and it's still cited in textbooks as the cautionary tale. When fit is weak, the extension usually fails — and worse, it can cause **brand dilution**, muddying the associations that made the parent brand valuable in the first place.

## In Everyday Life

Stand in the pain-relief aisle at a CVS or a Walgreens.

On the shelf: Tylenol Extra Strength, 500 mg acetaminophen. Next to it: the store's own brand — CVS Health or Walgreens — also 500 mg acetaminophen. Same active ingredient, same dose, both regulated by the FDA to the same standard. The store brand often costs noticeably less per caplet; the exact spread moves with sales and store, but a several-dollar gap on a 100-count bottle is typical.

Millions of Americans reach for the more expensive one anyway. That decision, repeated at scale, *is* brand equity. People aren't buying better chemistry. They're buying a reduction in doubt — at 2 a.m., with a sick kid, when you don't want to be the person who experimented.

Some of that trust was earned in a specific moment. In 1982, seven people in the Chicago area died after someone laced Tylenol capsules with cyanide. Johnson & Johnson pulled roughly 31 million bottles nationwide, went public fast, and came back with tamper-evident packaging that became the industry norm. The brand lost most of its share and rebuilt it within about a year. That's the double lesson: equity is fragile enough to nearly vanish in a week, and durable enough to be worth defending at enormous cost.

Now look one shelf over at the extensions: Tylenol PM. Tylenol Cold + Flu. Children's Tylenol. Every one of them is the same bet — *you already trust us with your headache, so trust us with your cold.* High perceived fit, so the borrowing works.

Then ask yourself the honest question: would you buy Tylenol-brand energy drinks? Same company, same trust, same shelf. But the fit collapses, and so would the extension. Tylenol means "makes discomfort go away safely." An energy drink means the opposite of sedation. The name would fight the product.

## Three-Line Recap

1. Brand equity is the value the name adds on top of the product — built from awareness, perceived quality, associations, and loyalty.
2. Brand identity is what you intend to mean; brand image is what customers actually think you mean, and the gap between them is the job.
3. Brand extensions let you spend accumulated equity in a new category — profitable when perceived fit is high, dilutive when it isn't.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** A store-brand acetaminophen has the identical active ingredient and dose as the national brand, yet many shoppers pay more for the national brand. This price premium is the clearest everyday evidence of:
- A) Product differentiation through formulation
- B) Brand equity
- C) A distribution advantage
- D) Regulatory protection

**2.** True or False: Brand identity and brand image mean the same thing.

**3.** A premium coffee brand launches branded ceramic mugs and travel tumblers. Compared with that same brand launching motor oil, the mug launch is more likely to succeed mainly because of:
- A) Lower manufacturing cost
- B) Higher perceived fit with existing brand associations
- C) Stronger patent position
- D) A larger addressable market

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Brand equity** — the added value a brand name gives a product beyond its functional attributes, visible as price premium, loyalty, and market power.
- **Brand identity** — the meaning and personality the company deliberately builds and wants the brand to stand for.
- **Brand image** — the meaning customers actually hold in their heads, which may differ from the intended identity.
- **Brand extension** — launching a product in a *new* category under an existing brand name (versus a **line extension**, a new variant inside the same category).
- **Brand dilution** — the weakening of a brand's core associations, typically caused by extensions that don't fit or by inconsistent quality.

---

*Answers: **1 — B.** With the active ingredient, dose, and regulatory standard held constant, the leftover willingness to pay is attributable to the name itself; that's the price-premium view of brand equity. **2 — False.** Identity is sender-side (what the firm intends); image is receiver-side (what the customer perceives). Managing a brand largely means shrinking the distance between the two. **3 — B.** Mugs and tumblers sit naturally inside a coffee brand's existing associations, so consumers transfer trust easily. Motor oil shares no meaningful associations with coffee, so the transfer fails and risks diluting the parent brand.*
